chapters.title: Chapter 4: The Legal and Regulatory Framework

lessons.title: Title, Encumbrance and Approvals: The Documents That Matter

children.text: Deepa pays a ₹15 lakh advance for a resale flat in Anna Nagar, Chennai. The seller shows her the sale deed, and the encumbrance certificate shows no loans. Three weeks later, a cooperative bank sends a notice: the seller had handed over the original title deeds as security for a business loan years ago, and the loan is unpaid. Nothing about that loan appeared in the documents Deepa checked. Property fraud in India rarely involves forged signatures. More often, it hides in the documents buyers do not know to ask for. This lesson shows you which ones matter.

body.text: A sale deed proves a sale happened. Title proves the seller had the right to sell. Approvals prove the building has the right to exist. You need all three before you pay.

children.text: The Three Layers of Property Due Diligence

body.caption: Every property check answers three questions

cells: Does the seller truly own it, with an unbroken chain of ownership?
Sale deeds going back about 30 years, mutation records, property tax receipts
Is it free of loans, charges, disputes and other claims?
Encumbrance certificate, CERSAI search, court case search, society dues
Was the land and building legally permitted and built as sanctioned?
Land use, building plan sanction, commencement certificate, occupancy certificate, RERA

children.text: Layer 1: Title

markDefs.definition: The legal right to own, use and transfer a property.
The sequence of documents showing every transfer of a property from the earliest traceable owner to the current seller.
The earliest or foundational document in a property's chain of title, from which later transfers can be traced.

children.text: The seller's own sale deed is only the last link. What you need is clear
title
, proven by an unbroken
chain of title
that traces ownership back through every previous sale, inheritance, gift or partition, ideally to a
mother deed
. A single missing link, such as a legal heir who never signed, can let someone challenge your ownership years later.

body.label: How far back to check
body.value: Typically about 30 years of ownership history
body.context: Lawyers and banks usually trace the chain of title for around 30 years. For land, inherited property or older layouts, going further back is often wise.

body.title: An illustrative chain of title: a flat in Whitefield, Bengaluru

events.title: Farmland bought by Mr Gowda
events.description: Registered sale deed from the original landowner. This becomes the mother deed for the lawyer's search.

events.title: Mr Gowda dies
events.description: His wife and three children inherit. A registered partition deed or proper succession documents are needed; a missing heir here is a classic future dispute.

events.title: Land converted and development agreement signed
events.description: The heirs convert the land to residential use and sign a joint development agreement with a developer.

events.title: Flat sold to Ms Rao
events.description: The developer and landowners sell a flat with its undivided share of land through a registered sale deed.

events.title: Resold to Mr Iyer
events.description: Registered resale deed; khata and property tax transferred to Mr Iyer's name.

events.title: Mr Iyer sells to you
events.description: Your lawyer must see every document above, not just Mr Iyer's 2020 deed.

cells: Names, property description and area match everything else
Each earlier owner had the right to sell
No gaps, and every seller in the chain was the recorded owner
Ownership passed correctly within a family
All legal heirs are accounted for and consented
Mutation or municipal record (khata, patta, property card)
Local records show the seller as owner for tax purposes
Name is updated and matches the sale deed
Taxes are paid and records are current
No arrears; receipts are in the seller's name
Any power of attorney used in the chain
Someone acted on the owner's behalf
It was registered, valid and specific to the transaction

body.text: Mutation records like khata, patta or property cards are revenue records. They show who pays tax, but on their own they do not prove ownership. Only a registered chain of title does. In Bengaluru, a verified e-khata has been required for property registration since July 2025, and a B-khata signals property with approval or tax irregularities that can affect loans and building permissions.

children.text: Layer 2: Encumbrances

markDefs.definition: Any legal claim or burden on a property, such as a mortgage, lien, lease, unpaid dues or pending dispute.
A document from the sub-registrar's office listing registered transactions on a property over a chosen period. A nil EC means no registered transactions were found for that period.
A mortgage created by handing over original title deeds to a lender as security, often without a registered mortgage deed.

children.text: An
encumbrance
is anything that burdens a property. The standard check is the
encumbrance certificate (EC)

, available online in many states through portals like TNREGINET in Tamil Nadu and Kaveri in Karnataka. But an EC only shows transactions that were registered. That is exactly how Deepa got caught: her seller had created an
equitable mortgage
by depositing title deeds with a bank, which never showed up on the EC.

body.title: What an encumbrance certificate shows and misses

columns.label: An EC typically shows
points: Registered sale deeds, gift deeds and partition deeds
Registered mortgage deeds and releases
Registered long-term leases
Other registered documents for the period searched

columns.label: An EC can miss
points: Mortgages created by depositing title deeds, where not registered
Unregistered agreements to sell or power of attorney deals
Pending court cases and family disputes
Unpaid property tax, society dues and utility bills

markDefs.definition: Central Registry of Securitisation Asset Reconstruction and Security Interest of India: a government registry where banks and financial institutions record security interests, including mortgages on property.

children.text: To close those gaps, add three more checks. Search
CERSAI

, where regulated lenders record charges on property, including many that never appear on an EC. Search the eCourts portal for cases involving the property or the seller's name. And publish a public notice in local newspapers inviting objections before you complete the purchase.

stats.label: CERSAI public search fee
stats.context: Search by property details or the borrower's name or PAN

stats.label: Typical title search period
stats.context: Longer for land and inherited property

body.title: Which check would have saved Deepa?
body.question: Deepa's EC showed no loans, but the seller had deposited the original title deeds with a cooperative bank as security. Which additional check was most likely to reveal the loan?
options: A CERSAI search on the property and the seller
body.explanation: Regulated lenders record security interests, including mortgages by deposit of title deeds, with CERSAI. An EC may not show them if no mortgage deed was registered. Asking to see the original title deeds, not photocopies, is another strong check: if the seller cannot produce them, find out why.

body.title: Name the certificate
body.textWithBlank: The document from the sub-registrar's office listing registered transactions on a property over a period is called an ___ certificate.
body.explanation: An encumbrance certificate shows registered transactions for the period searched. A nil EC is reassuring but not conclusive, because unregistered claims will not appear.

children.text: Layer 3: Approvals

markDefs.definition: Construction that differs from the sanctioned building plan, such as extra floors, larger built-up area or changed use.

children.text: Perfect title does not help if the building itself was never allowed. The Maradu flats in Kochi and the Supertech twin towers in Noida were demolished because of approval violations, not title problems. Approvals must exist, and the building on the ground must match them. Any
deviation
from the sanctioned plan, such as extra floors, can block an occupancy certificate or invite penalties and demolition.

body.caption: Approvals to verify for an apartment project

cells: The land is permitted for residential use
The number of floors, built-up area and layout allowed
Building has more floors than the sanction
Construction started before it was issued
Missing for a large project above the built-up area threshold
No registration number for a covered project
Built as sanctioned and fit to occupy
Keys handed over without an OC

body.text: A simple field test: count the floors. Then compare that number with the sanctioned building plan. If a plan approves ground plus 14 floors and you are standing in a 17-storey tower, the top three floors are a deviation, and every flat in the building may face problems getting an OC, utility connections or a clean resale.

children.text: Extra Documents for a Resale Flat
Original allotment letter and agreement
from the developer to the first buyer.
Society share certificate and NOC
confirming membership and no objection to the transfer.
No-dues letters
for society maintenance, property tax, electricity and water.
Loan closure letter and original documents
from the seller's bank, if the flat had a home loan.
Building OC
for the whole building, not just the seller's word that people live there.

body.title: "The bank approved the loan, so the property is fine"

columns.label: What a bank's approval does mean
points: The bank's lawyer and valuer found the property acceptable as security
Obvious title and approval problems were probably screened out
The bank believes the value supports the loan

columns.label: What it does not mean
points: The bank's checks protect the bank, not you
The review may be limited to what the bank needs
It does not guarantee against disputes, deviations or future demolition
It is no substitute for your own independent lawyer

body.title: The cheapest insurance you will buy
body.prompt: An independent property lawyer charges ₹25,000 to verify title, encumbrances and approvals for a ₹1.2 crore flat. What is the fee as a percentage of the flat's price? Round to two decimal places.
body.explanation: ₹25,000 ÷ ₹1,20,00,000 = 0.21%. For about a fifth of one percent, you protect the entire ₹1.2 crore. Compare that with the 7% or more you will pay in stamp duty on the same flat.

body.title: Deepa's next move
body.scenario: Deepa has paid a ₹15 lakh advance under an unregistered agreement for a ₹1.1 crore resale flat in Anna Nagar. She now learns the seller deposited the original title deeds with a cooperative bank for a business loan, which is in default. The seller says: "Don't worry, I will clear it with your remaining payment."
body.prompt: What should Deepa do now, and what should she have done differently?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Stop further payments: she should not pay any more until the loan is resolved and the bank releases the original title deeds.
2. Get legal advice immediately: an independent property lawyer should review her agreement, the bank's claim and her options to protect or recover the ₹15 lakh.
3. Verify the debt directly: she should confirm the outstanding amount with the bank itself, in writing, not rely on the seller's figures.
4. A safe structure, if she still wants the flat: pay the lender directly to close the loan, obtain the loan closure letter and original deeds, and register the sale deed at the same time, so her money never passes through the seller's hands.
5. What she should have done: asked to see the original title deeds before paying anything, run a CERSAI search, searched eCourts, published a public notice, and kept her advance small until checks were complete.
6. The broader lesson: a clean EC is necessary but not sufficient. Original documents plus CERSAI and court searches close most of the gaps.

body.title: Document Due Diligence Before Paying an Advance
steps: Inspect original title deeds, not photocopies
Get about 30 years of ownership documents, including inheritance and partition deeds
Obtain an encumbrance certificate for the full period
Run a CERSAI search on the property and the seller
Search eCourts for cases involving the property or the seller
Match mutation records and property tax receipts to the seller's name
Verify land use, building plan sanction, commencement certificate and OC
Compare the building on the ground with the sanctioned plan
For resale, collect society NOC, no-dues letters and any loan closure letter
Publish a public notice and have an independent lawyer sign off before paying

body.label: CERSAI: Public Search
body.description: Check whether a property or its owner has a security interest registered by a bank or financial institution.

cards.definition: The legal right to own, use and transfer a property.
The sequence of documents showing every ownership transfer, typically checked for about 30 years.
The foundational document from which a property's ownership history is traced.
A sub-registrar's record of registered transactions on a property over a chosen period.
A mortgage created by depositing original title deeds with a lender, which may not appear on an EC.
The central registry where lenders record security interests, searchable by the public for a small fee.
Construction that differs from the sanctioned building plan, such as unauthorised extra floors.

points: Due diligence has three layers: title (ownership), encumbrances (claims) and approvals (legality).
Check the full chain of title for about 30 years; mutation records alone do not prove ownership.
An encumbrance certificate shows only registered transactions; add CERSAI, eCourts searches and a public notice.
Always inspect original title deeds before paying; missing originals often mean a loan or a dispute.
Approvals must exist and match the building on the ground, since deviations can block OCs or lead to demolition.
A bank's loan approval protects the bank; hire your own independent lawyer, a tiny cost compared with the property's value.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not legal advice. Document names, registration systems and approval requirements vary by state and change over time, and the examples are illustrative. Always have a qualified, independent property lawyer verify title, encumbrances and approvals before paying any money.
